Okay, let's tackle this problem. So, the task is to look at four options of couplets in Persian poetry and figure out which one deviates in conceptual meaning or thematic message. The user wants me to focus on the underlying concepts, not the style or language.

First, I need to understand each couplet. Let me start with each one individually.

Option 1: "ناکس تربیت نشود ای حکیم کس - شمشیر نیک از آهن بد چون کند کسی؟"
Translating the key words: "na-kas tabeyat nashavad ay hakim kas" which might mean "O wise one, a bad nature cannot be tamed." Then the second line: "shamshir nik az ahan bad chun kand kas?" Maybe "How can a good sword be made from bad iron?" So, the message here seems to be that a bad nature can't be changed through upbringing, similar to how you can't make a good sword from bad iron. That's like saying inherent qualities can't be altered.

Option 2: "که چو تر شد پلیدتر باشد - سگ به دریای هفت گانه بشوی"
Second line: "dog goes into the sea of seven colors." The first line is "when it becomes clean, it becomes dirtier." Hmm, so if a dog (which is considered dirty in some contexts) washes in the sea, it becomes even dirtier. This is a metaphor for how trying to purify something inherently bad just makes it worse. So again, the idea that nature can't be changed through external means.

Option 3: "به سعی اندر او تربیت گم شود - ز وحشی نیاید که مردم شود"
First line: "Through effort in him, upbringing is lost." The second line: "From a wild one, a person will not come." So, if you try to raise a wild animal (or someone with a wild nature), you can't make them a human. This reinforces the idea that inherent wildness or bad nature can't be tamed through upbringing.

Option 4: "پی نیکان گرفت و مردم شد - سگ اصحاب کهف روزی چند"
First line: "He took the bread of the righteous and became a person." The second line: "The dog of the people of the cave, how many days..." Wait, the People of the Cave story in Islamic tradition includes a dog that stayed with them. The line here seems to say that the dog, after some days, became a person by taking the bread of the righteous. So this is suggesting that even a dog (symbolizing something not human or perhaps base) can become a person through association with the righteous. That's the opposite of the other options which say you can't change inherent nature.

So the common theme in options 1, 2, 3 is that upbringing or external efforts can't change a bad or wild nature. Option 4, however, presents a case where a dog (base nature) becomes a person through good company or actions. Therefore, option 4 is the one that deviates because it offers a positive transformation, while the others are about the futility of changing inherent traits.
